source: Kosinski (2023) Evaluating large language models in theory of mind tasks
finding: Older models solved no false-belief tasks. Newer GPT models solved a growing share. ChatGPT-4 was said to match 6-year-old children.
numbers: 40 false-belief tasks. davinci-002 5% (CI 0-10%); davinci-003 and ChatGPT-3.5-turbo 20%; ChatGPT-4 (June 2023) 75%.
limits: A task counts only if all controls pass. Success can come from text cues, not belief tracking. Perturbation studies (Ullman, Shapira) weaken the claim.
agent_relevance: Do not credit the agent with belief tracking from a pass on classic vignettes.

source: Kosinski (2023) controls and cue discussion
finding: The paper ran reversed-content, correct-label and true-belief controls and discusses that false-belief tasks can be solved without belief tracking.
numbers: Controls per task: unexpected-contents prompts plus true-belief controls; a task is solved only if every one is right.
limits: Authors' own account of the risk; text cues remain a rival explanation.
agent_relevance: Always include true-belief controls when testing the agent.

source: Ullman (2023) Large language models fail on trivial alterations to theory-of-mind tasks
finding: Tiny changes that keep the ToM logic make GPT-3.5 fail tasks it passed: a transparent bag, a label the protagonist cannot read, a protagonist who already knows the contents.
numbers: Unexpected contents: GPT-3.5 gave P(chocolate) about 87-98% in altered variants, still ascribing a false belief to Sam who cannot read the label. Transfer task: P(basket) 74-99% even when John saw the cat moved.
quote: small variations that maintain the principles of ToM turn the results on their head
limits: One author, one model (GPT-3.5), no human baseline. Strachan 2024 found humans also fail about half of the perceptual perturbations.
agent_relevance: Test the agent on perturbed variants. A pass on the standard form is weak evidence.

source: Ullman (2023) methodological conclusion
finding: Start from a skeptical baseline: outlying failures count for more than average success rates.
numbers: No new numbers beyond the vignette probabilities.
limits: Short note with a small item set.
agent_relevance: Use worst-case variants as the test, not the mean.

source: Shapira et al. (2023) Clever Hans or Neural Theory of Mind? Stress testing social reasoning in LLMs
finding: Six tasks. Models do well on standard false-belief items but break on adversarial ones, which suggests shallow heuristics.
numbers: GPT-4 97% on original ToM-k false-belief items. Adversarial categories: other-person 93.8% (davinci-002) down to 68.8% (GPT-4); inon 71.4% down to 0%; transparent access 66.7% down to 0%.
limits: Zero-shot, mostly OpenAI models. Multiple-choice probing differs slightly from LM probing. GPT-4 doing worse than older models on some adversarial classes is itself a boundary result.
agent_relevance: Newer or bigger does not mean more robust on social reasoning. Run adversarial sets.

source: Strachan et al. (2024) Testing theory of mind in large language models and humans (Nature Human Behaviour)
finding: Five-test ToM battery. GPT-4, GPT-3.5 and LLaMA2-70B each in 15 fresh chats, versus 1,907 humans in total. GPT-4 at or above humans on irony, hinting, strange stories and false belief; weak on faux pas.
numbers: Human N=1,907 (250 for the main battery). Irony: GPT-4 above humans (r=0.32, P=0.040); GPT-3.5 and LLaMA2-70B below. Strange stories: GPT-4 above humans (P=1.04e-5). Faux pas: the only test GPT-4 did not match humans, and the only one LLaMA2-70B beat humans.
limits: GPT models are closed and change over time. Text-only, English.
agent_relevance: A strong test design to copy: repeated fresh sessions, novel items, human baseline.

source: Strachan et al. (2024) faux pas follow-up variants
finding: Three explanations for GPT's faux pas failure were tested. Evidence favours hyperconservatism: GPT will not commit to 'the speaker did not know'. LLaMA2's win looked like a bias toward attributing ignorance.
numbers: In the quoted GPT-4 error pattern only 2 of 349 responses said the character knew. A likelihood-framed question ('more likely knew or did not know') was used to separate caution from inability.
limits: The likelihood variants are the authors' own new items; item counts are small.
agent_relevance: Phrase the question as a ranking of likelihoods. A hedged answer may hide a correct social inference.

source: Strachan et al. (2024) perturbation control with humans
finding: Replicated GPT's poor performance on Ullman-style perturbed false-belief items. Humans also failed half of the perturbations.
numbers: 757 human participants; humans failed half of the perturbation items; GPT models failed them too.
limits: Perturbations also change physics (transparency), so failure may not be a belief-tracking failure.
agent_relevance: Check a human baseline before calling an LLM failure a ToM failure.

source: Kim et al. (2023) FANToM: a benchmark for stress-testing machine theory of mind in interactions
finding: Conversations with information asymmetry. Models answer one belief question fairly well but are not consistent across six question types about the same fact.
numbers: Human ALL score 87.5. GPT-4 0613 + zero-shot CoT ALL* 26.6 (June) and 14.8 (Oct); ChatGPT 0613 + CoT 3.7; Llama-2 Chat + CoT 0.4; Flan-T5-XL fine-tuned 53.7. Models below humans by more than 70% on average.
quote: illusory or false sense of ToM capabilities in LLMs
limits: Only the zero-shot CoT prompt was tried. GPT-4 dropped between June and October runs (closed-model drift).
agent_relevance: Score the agent on consistency across question types. Single-question wins are 'illusory ToM'.

source: Kim et al. (2023) FANToM chain-of-thought and error analysis
finding: CoT improves most models but does not close the gap. CoT mainly lowers false positives (including an unaware character) and does not reliably lower false negatives.
numbers: Table 1: CoT raised scores but the gap to human 87.5 stayed large (GPT-4 June 26.6 on all question types). Some models lost score on the all-for-each-character metric after CoT.
limits: One CoT prompt only. Models are weak on list-type answerability questions yet do better on choice-type belief questions.
agent_relevance: A code-kept table of who knows what, per character, may beat prose reasoning.

source: Kim et al. (2023) FANToM fine-tuning result
finding: Fine-tuned Flan-T5-XL beats humans on single question types but not on the consistent all-types score.
numbers: Flan-T5-XL FT: ALL 53.7, answerability 55.9, info-access 54.4, against human 87.5, 90.6, 90.6.
limits: Benchmark not meant for training; training on it risks learning templates.
agent_relevance: A training-free scaffold should aim at consistency across questions, not single-question accuracy.

source: Wu et al. (2023) Hi-ToM: higher-order theory of mind benchmark
finding: Accuracy falls as belief nesting rises and with deceptive communication. Chain-of-thought gives no real gain.
numbers: All four models under 60% accuracy. GPT-4-32k vanilla 60.42 and 55.81 on the two story types (no deception / deception); CoT 64.04 and 55.72 (+3.60, -0.09). Joint accuracy at third order and above falls to about 0.05-0.35.
quote: CoTP prompting yields insignificant performance gains
limits: Templated English stories. Joint accuracy counts a high-order answer right only if all lower-order answers are right.
agent_relevance: Recursive belief past second order is beyond what the agent can be trusted with. Compute nesting in code.

source: Gandhi et al. (2023) Understanding social reasoning in language models with language models (BigToM)
finding: 5,000 model-written items with 25 controls. GPT-4 follows human inference patterns but less reliably. Most other models fail even forward belief. Backward belief (infer a belief from an action) is hardest.
numbers: Humans on backward belief: 82% true-belief, 72% false-belief. Most models far below chance there. Claude-2 0.675 / 0.708 vs gpt-4 0.858 / 0.861 on the Claude-made and GPT-4-made sets.
limits: Items were written by a model (GPT-4), so there is some circularity. Authors say copying the reasoning template may explain one-shot CoT gains.
agent_relevance: Models fail to infer beliefs from actions, which is what an agent needs when reading a user's behaviour.

source: Gandhi et al. (2023) BigToM prompt comparison
finding: Zero-shot CoT does not reliably help. One-shot examples help all models.
numbers: One-shot consistently better; zero-shot CoT inconsistent across conditions; one-shot CoT consistent gain but possibly by mimicry.
limits: Humans got instructions and an example, so the fair model comparison is one-shot.
agent_relevance: Keep one worked example in the slot prompt, not a generic 'think step by step'.

source: Wilf et al. (2023) Think Twice: perspective-taking improves LLM theory of mind (SimToM)
finding: Two-step prompt: first keep only what the character knows, then answer. Simulation theory used as a scaffold.
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo ToMI false belief +47 points over 0-shot CoT; BigToM false belief +29.5 over 0-shot and +14.2 over CoT; GPT-4 ToMI false belief +13.4 but slight drop on BigToM.
quote: simple solutions to ToM still elude us
limits: BigToM was made by GPT-4, which may confound the GPT-4 result. Model-made perspective filters sometimes invent facts.
agent_relevance: Direct candidate operator: a separate perspective-filter call before answering about another mind.

source: Wilf et al. (2023) SimToM ablations and oracle perspective
finding: Oracle perspective beats model-made perspective, so the filter step itself errs. A single-prompt version loses much of the gain.
numbers: Oracle: ToMI false belief 81.0 to 96; BigToM false belief 70.5 to 96.0. Single-prompt variant reduced BigToM total to 58.25 (17.63 below 0-shot CoT).
limits: GPT-3.5-Turbo only for the ablations.
agent_relevance: Keep the perspective step in its own call and check it where code can.

source: Wilf et al. (2023) SimToM domain-specific examples
finding: Adding domain-specific perspective-taking examples lifts results again.
numbers: BigToM false belief 70.5% to 90.5% (+20 points, +34.25 over 0-shot CoT); ToMI all questions 72.8 to 79.3.
limits: Tuned prompts risk overfitting to benchmark templates.
agent_relevance: Gains are larger when the domain structure is known.

source: Wilf et al. (2023) SimToM versus other prompting methods
finding: Self-consistency CoT and Tree-of-Thoughts did not match perspective-taking on false belief.
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo false belief: SC-CoT 33.50% vs SimToM 81.00%.
limits: Tree-of-Thoughts voting was built for creative writing, a poor fit.
agent_relevance: Majority vote over samples (G4) does not repair a missing perspective step.

source: Wang and Zhao (2023) Metacognitive prompting improves understanding in large language models
finding: Five-step prompt copied from human metacognition: understand, first judgement, critical evaluation, final decision with reasons, confidence. Beat CoT and plan-and-solve on ten NLU tasks.
numbers: GPT-4 zero-shot MP 89.9/86.2 vs CoT 88.9/84.7 on one dataset; 64.0 vs 54.7 on another; 5-shot gains over CoT-SC about 2.2-3.5 points; 4.8-6.4 over CoT in some model sets.
limits: Language understanding tasks only, not social. Gains small for GPT-4, which is near ceiling.
agent_relevance: Fixed introspection steps help understanding tasks. See the overthinking error cost.

source: Wang and Zhao (2023) MP error analysis
finding: Where metacognitive prompting fails: it overthinks.
numbers: Overthinking errors 68.3%; overcorrection errors 31.7% of MP errors; overcorrection mostly on tasks needing nuanced judgement.
limits: Error counts from an analysis sample, not the whole test set.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that always-on reflection can flip right answers, in line with G1.

source: Huang et al. (2023) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Self-review with no outside signal does not help and often hurts. With an oracle label the correction looks great.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 after round 1 and 41.8 after round 2; GSM8K 75.9 to 74.7; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0, HotpotQA 49 to 43. With oracle label GPT-4 GSM8K 97.5, HotpotQA 59.0. GPT-3.5 kept its GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time.
quote: LLMs struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback
limits: Three benchmarks, two OpenAI models. Oracle numbers use ground truth, so they are not real gains.
agent_relevance: Supports G1 and G2: metacognitive review needs a real failing signal. Clinical rumination is similar: going over a thought without new information does not help.

source: Sharma et al. (2023) Cognitive reframing of negative thoughts through human-language model interaction
finding: Retrieval-enhanced in-context GPT-3 writes reframed thoughts. A randomized field study on a mental health site tested which reframes help.
numbers: 600 practitioner-written examples; 2,067 participants; 11.2% higher BLEU and 9.7% higher ROUGE. Higher-empathy reframes preferred 39.7% vs 25.5%; higher specificity 39.2% vs 27.4%; more positive reframes preferred 22.7% less often (29.6% vs 38.3%). Rational reframes 10.8% more relatable; ones addressing thinking traps 6.3% more helpful.
limits: GPT-3, 2023. Outcomes are self-rated relatability, helpfulness and memorability, not symptom change. Of flagged reframes 59% were generic and 16% made wrong assumptions.
agent_relevance: Positivity alone does not help; specific, rational, actionable reframes do.

source: CBT-Bench authors (2024) CBT-Bench: evaluating large language models on assisting cognitive behavior therapy
finding: Three levels: knowledge questions, cognitive-model understanding (distortions, core beliefs), and therapeutic response. Models do well on facts and poorly on fine-grained labels.
numbers: Level I 220 test questions: Llama-3.1-405B 95.0, GPT-4o 94.1, Llama-3.1-8B 78.2, human experts 90.7. Level II: 146 distortion, 184 core-belief, 112 fine-grained examples; human expert F1 49.1, 77.7, 54.6, model scores low. Level III 156 exercises: Llama-3.1-405B -0.01, Llama-3.1-8B -0.22, GPT-4o -0.32 on a -2 to 2 scale against the reference.
limits: Six models, only three at Level III, no controlled prompt ablation, small expert-labelled sets. Per-cell Level II model F1 was not verified.
agent_relevance: Labelling the belief behind a thought is where LLMs are weakest. Do not use a model to diagnose a belief type without a check.

source: CRBot study (2025) Evaluating an LLM-powered chatbot for cognitive restructuring
finding: GPT-4 chatbot with a system prompt and 10 few-shot examples kept the exploration, evaluation, substitution phases. Clinicians found toxic positivity, leading questions and misread emotions.
numbers: 19 users (mean age 20); 95 dialogs reviewed by 4 clinicians; mean 7.6 user turns; baseline PHQ-9 5.57, GAD-7 5.19. 'Embarrassed' became 'tough'; 'maybe' was treated as agreement.
limits: Small, young, mildly distressed sample. Qualitative. No symptom outcomes.
agent_relevance: A fixed phase script keeps dialog on track, but the model misreads tone, so a program should check phase state.

source: Normann and Morina (2018) The efficacy of metacognitive therapy: a systematic review and meta-analysis
finding: Human clinical baseline for Wells' approach. Very large effects against waitlist, medium against other active treatments, shrinking at follow-up.
numbers: 25 trials, 780 patients, 15 RCTs. Vs waitlist (k=9) Hedges g=2.06 (CI 1.52-2.60). Vs CBT and other active (k=8) g=0.69 post, 0.37 at follow-up (CI 0.07-0.66). Trim-and-fill corrected g=0.53. Only 5 of 15 controlled trials described allocation concealment.
limits: Few trials, thin follow-up data, publication-bias risk.
agent_relevance: Context only. No LLM test of MCT was found.

source: Liu et al. (2026) Metacognition in LLMs: foundations, progress, and opportunities
finding: Broad overview of LLM metacognition: how to measure it, raise it, apply it. Only the abstract page was read.
numbers: No figures read.
limits: Abstract only. Not checked whether it covers social or clinical metacognition.
agent_relevance: Check the full text for newer evidence before building a social-metacognition operator.

source: Targeted search for LLM tests of Wells' metacognitive therapy (negative result)
finding: One shared web search found no paper applying Wells' MCT to an LLM or chatbot. Only CBT-style tools turned up.
numbers: 0 MCT-LLM papers from one targeted search; CBT tools found: CRBot, CBT-Bench, CBT-LLM.
limits: One US-only search; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate-limited. Absence is not proof.
agent_relevance: Possible gap: no one seems to have tested 'what do you believe about this thought?' prompts in agents.

source: Transfer of the MCT idea to agents (our own analysis, not a source)
finding: MCT changes beliefs about thinking (for example 'worrying helps'), not thought content. The closest agent analogue is a rule about its own process, such as 'longer reasoning is always better'. No tested system does this.
numbers: No measured result. Related own result cited in SCHEMA G1: forced doubt cut word-puzzle accuracy from 92% to 75%.
limits: Inference by analogy only.
agent_relevance: Maps to G1: doubt only on a signal. Social and clinical metacognition mostly does not transfer beyond the perspective filter.
